sourceReview: Read bundled BSB Psalm 60 in full with each verse's related passages before drafting. References are thematic or literary comparisons, not an invented historical occasion. Scripture is never stored in the notes; it loads from the bundled BSB.

study.title: With God we will perform with valor.
study.intro: Twelve verses lament a defeat that shook the land like an earthquake, recall God's word claiming the tribes and neighboring lands as His, and end trusting that human help is worthless but God gives valor.
study.context: The heading names David, the tune 'The Lily of the Covenant,' and a setting during David's wars with Aram-naharaim and Aram-zobah, when Joab struck down Edomites in the Valley of Salt. 2 Samuel 8:3–14 and 1 Chronicles 18:3–13 record these campaigns; the numbers differ between accounts (18,000 in 2 Samuel 8:13 and 1 Chronicles 18:12, 12,000 here), likely reflecting different reports of the same campaign. The psalm itself laments a setback, perhaps an Edomite invasion while the army was away. Verses 1–5 describe God's rejection and plead for help; verses 6–8 quote God's word claiming Israel's tribal lands and Moab, Edom and Philistia; verses 9–12 ask who will lead them and trust in God. Verses 5–12 are reused in Psalm 108:6–13. The place names describe David's era; the notes do not treat them as claims about modern borders or peoples. The Scripture is loaded unchanged from the bundled BSB, including the heading.
study.peopleNote: David is named in the heading; his profile includes his wars and the expansion of his kingdom. Joab is named in the heading but has no profile in the app. Planned paintings show a cracked landscape, a banner, a basin, a sandal and a fortified city, with no battle scenes or gore; God is never portrayed as a human body.

verses.title: Restore us
verses.heading: Lament after defeat
verses.meaning: The heading names David and sets the psalm during his wars with the Arameans and Joab's victory over Edom in the Valley of Salt. Yet the psalm opens with lament: God has rejected and broken His people. He has been angry. The people cry, 'Restore us!' Perhaps a setback came before victory, such as an attack from Edom while David's army was in the north. The verse names defeat as God's doing and appeals to Him to turn back.
verses.context: 2 Samuel 8:3–14 records David's victories over Zobah, Aram and Edom, and 1 Kings 11:15–16 mentions Joab's campaign in Edom. Psalm 60:1 laments a setback within that period.
explore: You have rejected us
The people feel cast off. They attribute the defeat to God's anger.
Restore us
They ask God to turn toward them again. The plea is for renewed favor.
verses.reflect: Where do you need God to restore you after a setback?
verses.alt: A broken city gate hangs open on a dusty road at dawn.

verses.title: Heal its fractures
verses.heading: A land torn as by earthquake
verses.meaning: You have shaken the land and torn it open. Heal its fractures, for it is quaking. The defeat feels like an earthquake. The land is split, cracked and trembling. The image may be metaphorical, describing national chaos, or it may recall an actual tremor. The people ask God to heal the breaks. Only the One who shook the land can mend it.
verses.context: Amos 1:1 dates the prophet's ministry by an earthquake, and Isaiah 24:19–20 describes the earth split and shaken. 2 Chronicles 7:14 promises that God will heal the land of a repentant people.
explore: Torn it open
The land is split. The disaster feels like an earthquake.
Heal its fractures
Only God can mend the land. The people ask Him to repair it.
verses.reflect: What feels broken in your community or life? How could you ask God to heal it?
verses.alt: A deep crack runs across a field of grain under a grey sky.

verses.title: The wine of staggering
verses.heading: Hardship from God's hand
verses.meaning: You have shown Your people hardship; we are staggered from the wine You made us drink. The people describe their trouble as a cup of wine that makes them stagger. In the prophets, the 'cup of God's wrath' describes judgment that leaves nations reeling (Isaiah 51:17). The people feel dizzy and disoriented. The image names how confusing and overwhelming defeat can be.
verses.context: Isaiah 51:17 speaks of the cup that makes people stagger, and Jeremiah 25:15–16 describes the cup of the wine of wrath. Psalm 60:3 feels that cup in defeat.
explore: Shown hardship
The people have seen difficult things. God has let them suffer.
Staggered
They are dizzy and disoriented. The defeat has shaken them.
verses.reflect: When have you felt staggered by hardship? How did you find your footing?
verses.alt: A tipped cup spills dark wine across a tilted table.

verses.title: A banner for those who fear You
verses.heading: A rallying point
verses.meaning: You have raised a banner for those who fear You, that they may flee the bow. Selah. God has raised a banner, a flag on a pole, for His people. In war, a banner showed where to gather. Here it may be a rallying point to escape the archers. The verse offers the first hope in the psalm. God provides a place to regroup. Selah pauses.
verses.context: Exodus 17:15 records Moses naming an altar 'The LORD Is My Banner,' and Isaiah 11:10–12 pictures a banner raised for the nations. Psalm 60:4 sees God's banner as a place of refuge.
explore: A banner
A flag marks where to gather. God provides a rallying point.
Flee the bow
The banner offers escape. Those who fear God can find safety.
verses.reflect: What is your rallying point when life feels like a battle?
verses.alt: A tall plain banner flies over a hilltop at sunset.

verses.title: Your beloved
verses.heading: A plea for rescue
verses.meaning: Respond and save us with Your right hand, that Your beloved may be delivered. The people ask God to answer and save them with His right hand, symbol of strength. They call themselves 'Your beloved.' Despite feeling rejected, they still claim God's love. The plea rests on that relationship. Psalm 108:6 begins its reuse of this psalm here.
verses.context: Deuteronomy 33:12 calls Benjamin 'the beloved of the LORD,' and Psalm 108:6 repeats this verse as the start of its reused section. Psalm 60:5 holds onto love even in defeat.
explore: Your right hand
God's strength is sought. His right hand is the image of the power that saves.
Your beloved
The people still claim God's love. Relationship grounds their plea.
verses.reflect: Even in hardship, how could you remember you are God's beloved?
verses.alt: A sheltering hand-shaped rock overhang protects a small spring.

verses.title: God has spoken
verses.heading: Shechem and Succoth
verses.meaning: God has spoken from His sanctuary: 'I will triumph! I will parcel out Shechem and apportion the Valley of Succoth.' Now God's own word is quoted, perhaps a prophetic oracle given at the sanctuary. God speaks like a victorious warrior dividing land. Shechem lies west of the Jordan, Succoth east of it. Both are linked to Jacob (Genesis 33:17–18). God claims both sides of the river as His to give. The notes read this as God's word for David's time, not as a modern territorial claim.
verses.context: Genesis 33:17–18 records Jacob building shelters at Succoth and then arriving at Shechem. Joshua 24:1 records Israel renewing the covenant at Shechem. Psalm 60:6 reaffirms God's ownership of these lands.
explore: From His sanctuary
God speaks from His holy place. The word carries His authority.
Shechem and Succoth
Places west and east of the Jordan. God claims both.
verses.reflect: What promise of God could anchor you when circumstances seem to deny it?
verses.alt: Surveyors' cords stretch across a valley between two hills.

verses.title: Judah is My scepter
verses.heading: The tribes as God's armor
verses.meaning: 'Gilead is Mine, and Manasseh is Mine; Ephraim is My helmet, Judah is My scepter.' God continues naming His territory. Gilead and part of Manasseh lay east of the Jordan. Ephraim, a strong northern tribe, is His helmet, His defense. Judah, David's tribe, is His scepter, the symbol of royal rule. Genesis 49:10 says the scepter will not depart from Judah. God pictures His people as His own royal armor.
verses.context: Genesis 49:10 says the scepter will not depart from Judah, and Deuteronomy 33:17 describes Ephraim's strength. Psalm 60:7 pictures the tribes as God's armor and royal insignia.
explore: Ephraim is My helmet
The strong northern tribe guards the head. Ephraim is pictured as God's defense.
Judah is My scepter
David's tribe rules. The scepter symbolizes kingship.
verses.reflect: What does it mean to belong to God as part of His people?
verses.alt: A bronze helmet and a gold scepter rest on a map-like carpet.

verses.title: Moab My washbasin
verses.heading: Neighboring lands under God
verses.meaning: 'Moab is My washbasin; upon Edom I toss My sandal; over Philistia I shout in triumph.' God names the surrounding nations. Moab becomes a washbasin, a humble household object. Throwing a sandal over something may signify taking possession (compare Ruth 4:7). Philistia hears God's victory shout. The images describe these nations as subject to God's rule in David's era. They are poetic royal language for the time, not statements about any people today.
verses.context: Ruth 4:7 records removing a sandal to confirm a transaction, and 2 Samuel 8:2, 12–14 records David's dominance over Moab, Edom and Philistia. Psalm 60:8 uses household images for God's sovereignty.
explore: My washbasin
A humble household item. Moab is pictured as serving God.
Toss My sandal
The gesture may mean possession. Edom is under God's rule.
verses.reflect: How does knowing God rules over all nations shape how you see the world?
verses.alt: A bronze washbasin sits on a floor with a sandal tossed beside it.

verses.title: Who will lead me to Edom?
verses.heading: Seeking a leader
verses.meaning: Who will bring me to the fortified city? Who will lead me to Edom? The speaker, probably David or the king, asks who will lead him into Edom's strongholds. Edom's cities were built in rugged mountains and were hard to conquer. The question is not despair but a search for God's help. The next verse explains why the answer must be God.
verses.context: Obadiah 1:3 describes Edom living in the clefts of the rock with its dwelling on high, and 2 Samuel 8:14 records garrisons in Edom. Psalm 60:9 asks who can lead the way there.
explore: Fortified city
Edom's cities were strong. They were hard to reach.
Who will lead me?
The king looks for guidance. No human general can lead him there without God.
verses.reflect: What seemingly impossible challenge do you need God to lead you through?
verses.alt: A fortress city clings to red sandstone cliffs.

verses.title: Will You no longer march out?
verses.heading: The lament returns
verses.meaning: Have You not rejected us, O God? Will You no longer march out, O God, with our armies? The question of verse 1 returns. Has God really rejected them? Will He not go out with their armies? The speaker remembers past victories when God led Israel. Now He seems absent. The question is painful, but it is also hopeful. It assumes that God's going out is what makes the difference.
verses.context: Psalm 44:9 says, 'You no longer go forth with our armies,' and 2 Samuel 5:24 records God going out before David. Psalm 60:10 asks the same question.
explore: Have You not rejected us?
The question repeats verse 1. Lament returns even after God's word of victory.
March out with our armies
God's presence decides battles. The speaker longs for it.
verses.reflect: When God feels absent, what do you remember about how He has led before?
verses.alt: An army camp waits in silence with its standard pole empty.

verses.title: The help of man is worthless
verses.heading: Turning to God alone
verses.meaning: Give us aid against the enemy, for the help of man is worthless. The speaker asks God for help and admits that human help is useless. Alliances and armies cannot save. Only God's aid matters. This is not a rejection of human effort but a statement about where true deliverance comes from. It echoes Psalm 146:3: 'Do not put your trust in princes.'
verses.context: Psalm 146:3 says, 'Do not put your trust in princes, in man, who cannot save,' and Jeremiah 17:5 warns against trusting in man. Psalm 60:11 turns to God alone.
explore: Give us aid
The plea is direct. The people need God's help against an enemy they cannot face alone.
Help of man is worthless
Human alliances and armies cannot finally save. Only God's aid makes the difference.
verses.reflect: Where have you been relying on human help more than God?
verses.alt: A broken reed staff lies beside a sturdy rock on a path.

verses.title: With God we will perform with valor
verses.heading: Confidence restored
verses.meaning: With God we will perform with valor, and He will trample our enemies. The psalm ends with confidence. With God, the people will act bravely. It is God who will defeat the enemies. The final word moves from lament to trust. Valor is real, but it depends on God. The victory belongs to Him. Psalm 108:13 repeats this ending.
verses.context: Psalm 108:13 repeats this verse, and Philippians 4:13 says, 'I can do all things through Christ who gives me strength.' Psalm 60:12 ends the lament in trust.
explore: With God
Valor depends on God's presence. The people act bravely because He is with them.
He will trample
The victory belongs to God. He defeats the enemies.
verses.reflect: What would it look like to act bravely with God in a challenge you face?
verses.alt: A banner rises again over a restored gate at sunrise.
